content: Approximately one in three individuals in the United States will develop shingles, also known as herpes zoster, at some point in their lifetime. Shingles can sometimes result in severe complications, such as persistent nerve pain (postherpetic neuralgia) or vision loss. Vaccination is the most effective way to protect yourself from shingles. Shingles is a painful condition characterized by a rash. It occurs when the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), the same virus responsible for chickenpox, reactivates in the body after a person has previously had chickenpox. Each year, an estimated one million people in the United States are affected by shingles. Most individuals experience shingles only once in their lifetime, but it is possible to have it more than once. The most common presentation of shingles is a rash that appears on one side of the body, either the left or the right. This rash is often accompanied by pain, itching, or a tingling sensation. Shingles can lead to complications, with the most frequent being postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), a type of long-term nerve pain. Individuals are at risk for shingles if they have previously had chickenpox. Over 99% of Americans born before 1980 have had chickenpox, even if they do not recall it. While shingles can occur in children, it is uncommon. The risk of developing shingles and experiencing severe complications increases with age, in individuals with weakened immune systems due to medical conditions (e.g., certain cancers like leukemia or lymphoma, or HIV infection), or in those taking immunosuppressive medications such as steroids or drugs used after organ transplantation. Shingles is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, which remains dormant in the body after a person has had chickenpox. The virus can reactivate later in life, leading to shingles. It is important to note that shingles itself is not contagious; however, individuals who have never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine can contract the varicella-zoster virus from someone with shingles. This can occur through direct contact with fluid from shingles blisters or by inhaling virus particles from the blisters. These individuals may then develop chickenpox, which could later lead to shingles. The most effective way to prevent shingles is through vaccination. The CDC recommends two doses of the recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV, Shingrix) for adults aged 50 years and older to prevent shingles and its complications. Shingrix is also recommended for adults aged 19 years and older who have weakened immune systems due to disease or therapy. If you have shingles, you can take steps to reduce the risk of spreading the virus to others. Covering the rash, avoiding touching or scratching it, washing your hands frequently for at least 20 seconds, and avoiding contact with certain individuals (e.g., pregnant individuals who have never had chickenpox or the vaccine, premature or low birth weight infants, and people with weakened immune systems) can help prevent transmission. The virus cannot be spread before the blisters appear or after the rash has scabbed over. Several antiviral medications, including acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, are available to treat shingles. These medications can reduce the duration and severity of the illness and are most effective when started as soon as the rash appears. If you suspect you have shingles, it is important to contact your healthcare provider promptly to discuss treatment options. Pain relief medications, whether over-the-counter or prescription, may help alleviate the discomfort associated with shingles. Additionally, wet compresses, calamine lotion, and warm oatmeal baths can provide relief from itching.
